bodyMarkdown:
Paducah stands where the Tennessee River meets the Ohio, in the Jackson Purchase region of western Kentucky. The land had been part of the [Chickasaw hunting grounds](/stories/chickasaw-hunting-grounds/). The 1818 [Jackson Purchase treaty](https://grokipedia.com/page/Paducah,_Kentucky) transferred Chickasaw holdings in western Kentucky to the United States for $200,000.

## From Pekin to Paducah

The brothers James and William Pore settled the site of [Paducah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paducah,_Kentucky) around 1821 and called it "Pekin." In 1827 William Clark laid out a town there and renamed it Paducah. Clark had been co-leader of the Lewis and Clark Expedition and was then superintendent of Indian affairs.

## Where the name came from

Accounts of the name disagree. One account notes that local lore long tied it to a Chickasaw chief named "Paduke." But experts on the Chickasaw say no chief or tribe of that name ever existed, and the Chickasaw language has no related words. Historians instead believe Clark named the town for the Comanche of the western plains, whom settlers called the Padoucas.

Another account gives more weight to the local tradition. It describes Paduke as a Chickasaw band leader whose people kept a village near the site until the Jackson Purchase. It also cites the writer Irvin S. Cobb, a Paducah native, who traced the name to a Chickasaw phrase meaning "a place where the grapes hang down."

## River town

Paducah was established as a town in 1830. Its place at the meeting of two rivers made it a trading center. Steamboats carried tobacco, corn and lumber downstream to markets such as New Orleans, and by the 1840s the town was a regional commercial center.

## Civil War and General Order No. 11

Kentucky tried to stay neutral when the Civil War began. When Confederate troops occupied Columbus, Union forces under Gen. Ulysses S. Grant responded by occupying Paducah. For most of the war it served as a huge Union supply depot.

On December 17, 1862, under Grant's General Order No. 11, Union forces made 30 Jewish families leave their homes in Paducah. The order rested on antisemitic stereotypes about the cotton black market. Local businessman Cesar Kaskel protested to President Lincoln and met with him, and Lincoln had the order revoked within a few weeks.

## The 1937 flood

The Ohio River flood of 1937 was the worst natural disaster in Paducah's history. The river crested at 60.8 feet on February 2, and about 27,000 residents had to flee. Afterward, Congress had the Army Corps of Engineers build the floodwall that now protects the city.

## Kentucky today

Paducah is the seat of McCracken County and had 27,137 people in 2020. Twenty blocks of its downtown are a historic district on the National Register. The National Quilt Museum opened there in 1991, and the city joined the UNESCO Creative Cities Network for craft and folk art in 2013.
